NASA leadership takes the podium today for what could be the most important Moon-program briefing in years. The space agency is holding a media briefing titled “Artemis Acceleration” at 2 p.m. Eastern — 1 p.m. Central — at the Kennedy Space Center in Florida, with an update on its plans to return American astronauts to the surface of the Moon by 2028.

NASA announced the briefing in a media advisory on October 14. On the dais: NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman, Associate Administrator Amit Kshatriya, and Artemis program manager Jeremy Parsons. The briefing will stream live on nasa.gov/live.

According to the agency’s advisory, the update will include details on Artemis III — the mission NASA describes as sending four astronauts into low Earth orbit next year to test the critical systems needed for future lunar landings, rather than a trip to the Moon itself — and on how the plans for a crewed return to the lunar surface by 2028 are progressing. The agency has previously said Artemis III will test rendezvous and docking between the Orion capsule and two competing human-rated lunar landers: SpaceX’s Starship and Blue Origin’s Blue Moon. The next step, Artemis IV, is targeted to deliver astronauts to the Moon’s south pole in early 2028.

What to watch for — and what to be skeptical of

Hardware is moving: an Artemis III solid rocket booster now stands in the Vehicle Assembly Building’s High Bay 3 at Kennedy, a milestone NASA tied directly to today’s briefing. But the 2028 landing target faces real questions. The Congressional Research Service has flagged that both commercial lander providers face schedule delays and technical risks that could threaten NASA’s stated timeline.

This briefing is a follow-up to the program overhaul Administrator Isaacman announced publicly in February 2026 — so today may sharpen plans already on the table rather than unveil something entirely new. NASA’s own advisory does not announce new dates, hardware, or mission changes; it commits the agency only to a progress report. Readers should treat any claim about what will be announced today as speculation until the briefing takes place.

Three questions frame the session: how firm the 2028 landing goal really is, what Artemis III must demonstrate in orbit, and how NASA sequences the missions after it. For students and space watchers across Webb County and the border region, the livestream is the way to hear it first

title: NASA Briefs 'Artemis Acceleration' Plans Today as It Targets a 2028 Moon Landing
